[Diaporthe] Symptoms:
Diaporthe on soybean exhibits distinctive symptoms primarily on stems, leaves, and pods, characterized by dark brown to black lesions that are typically sunken and have raised margins. These lesions can vary in size and shape but often present as irregular patches ranging from a few millimeters to several centimeters in diameter. Affected tissues may show a discolored, leathery appearance, with some areas exhibiting a glossy, dark coating of mycelium at high humidity conditions. Occasionally, small, pinpoint black pycnidia can emerge at the center of the lesions, contributing to a spotted appearance. Leaf symptoms may manifest as angular lesions bordered by yellow halos, while pod infections can lead to shrivelled seeds and reduced quality. This disease can also cause wilting and premature death of infected tissues, giving plants a scorched look. Unlike Phomopsis, which features smaller, more uniform lesions predominantly on leaves, Diaporthe lesions display irregular shapes and are more pervasive across various plant parts. | Often confused with: Diaporthe_2015_Kanawha

[Sudden_death_syndrome] Symptoms:
Foliar symptoms of sudden death syndrome (SDS) are caused by a toxin produced by the fungus, moving from roots to the leaves. Initially, leaves of infected plants exhibit scattered yellow spots between leaf veins. These spots develop into larger chlorotic and necrotic blotches, while the midvein and major lateral veins remain green. Eventually, leaflets drop, but petioles remain on the stem. Diseased plants typically have rotted taproots and lateral roots, with the outer tissue of the taproot appearing brown. When stems are split lengthwise, the discoloration of the woody tissue can be light gray to brown and may extend up to two inches above ground. The presence of bluish fungal growth on the roots can be observed if soil moisture is high. Notably, the foliar symptoms of SDS resemble those of brown stem rot, but key differences exist in internal stem browning, as SDS-infected stems maintain white pith, while brown stem rot causes brown discoloration. A key difference is that the internal stem condition of plants with sudden death syndrome shows white pith, differing from the brown discoloration characteristic of brown stem rot.
